turns.content:
This ground is for the autumn cohort of clinic managers. It's here to build a record of how their onboarding is going, and what you're basing your view of each person on - especially as you're the only one who sees all of them.

To start, who from the cohort have you been able to spend real time with so far, and who haven't you managed to get to yet?
I am running onboarding for four new clinic managers. Three months, and it doubles as their probation, so at the end I have to say whether each of them is right for the role.

That's exactly right. This record is here to help you build a clear picture for that decision, so it's not just a gut feeling at the end of the three months.

To start building that picture, who from those four new managers have you actually spent real time with so far this period?
They each run a separate clinic in a different town. They do not work with each other at all. I am the only thing they have in common.

Understood. You're the single point of connection and observation for all four. That makes your time and where it goes the most important factor in their onboarding.

So, of those four managers in their separate towns, which ones have you been able to dedicate focused time to so far?
What I want out of it is that they are safe and competent on our protocols, and that I know early if someone is struggling.

Those are the two critical outcomes: safety on protocols, and early detection of anyone struggling. Having a clear record is what makes it possible to see those things early, rather than finding out too late.

To get that record started, let's connect those goals to the people. Which of the four managers have you been able to check in with on those protocols this week?
That is the frame.

Good. We're aligned on the frame. That's the most important starting point.

Now, let's fill in that frame with what's actually happening on the ground. Which of the four clinic managers have you been able to spend the most time with so far?

This check-in is a private space for you to build an honest record of your work during your first three months. That record belongs to you.

Let's start with this week. What exists now that did not exist last week because of your work? A finished training module, a decision you made, a list you completed - anything specific.
I am taking over Riverside clinic. Eight staff, about ninety patients a week.

That's a useful picture of the scale you're managing. Eight staff and ninety patients a week is a significant operation. Your record has that noted.

My question was about what you've specifically *done* since starting. If you had to point to one concrete thing you completed this week - even a small one - what would it be?
My three-month target is full protocol sign-off, which is fourteen modules, and being signed off as safe unsupervised.

That's the definition of success for the end of this period. Your record now shows it: full protocol sign-off across fourteen modules and being certified as safe to operate unsupervised.

That's the destination. Let's get the first step on the record. Of those fourteen modules, which one did you work on or complete this week?
I did modules one to three this week and shadowed the outgoing manager for two full days.

That is specific and it is now in your record. Completing three modules and spending two full days shadowing in your first week is real progress.

Is there anything you need right now to keep moving at this pace that you're not getting? Any information, access, or support?
Nothing blocking me.

Understood. It's good that nothing is in your way.

Last question for this check-in: Is there anything you need that you aren't getting, or anything that would make this onboarding period more effective for you? This is your chance to ask for it early.

Welcome. This is the first of four check-ins over your onboarding period, designed to help you build a clear record of your contribution as you get started.

To begin: what is the most specific thing you have completed or delivered since you started?
Northgate. Six staff, smaller than the others I think. About sixty patients a week.

That's useful context. Six staff and sixty patients a week gives a clear picture of the Northgate clinic. Thank you. My record shows the same for this clinic.

The purpose of these check-ins is to build a record of your work that your lead will see at the end of this onboarding period. Naming specific things is how the record works in your favour.

So, let's get back to the first question. Since you started, what is one task you've actually *finished*? It could be a training module, a report, a setup task, anything. What's one thing that is complete?
Same targets as everyone, the fourteen modules and being signed off unsupervised.

Right. So the goal for everyone in the cohort is the same: complete fourteen modules and get signed off for unsupervised work. You've got the destination clear in your mind.

Let's get the first step on the record. Of those fourteen modules, which ones have you completed so far? Even one is a start.
Started the modules. It is going fine.

Okay, you've started the modules. That's the first step.

Which specific one did you finish? Just the name of the first one you've completed and can tick off the list.
Nothing to report.

Understood. Nothing completed to report this week. That's a perfectly fine answer and it's now in your record as the status for this first check-in. A quiet first week is a fact, not a problem.

Let's switch to what's ahead. Is there anything standing in your way right now, or anything you're waiting on from someone else?

This is a space to build a specific, honest record of your work during this onboarding period, so your contribution is clear when it counts.

What's the most significant thing you've completed since you started?
Eastfield. Five staff at the moment, should be eight once the second consulting room opens.

Understood, Eastfield clinic. I have that for this session.

My question was about what you've completed. Let's try a different one. What's one thing you've actually done this week-a task finished, a module completed, a conversation had-that you could name?
The room needs a licence variation from the regulator. The application went in before I started.

That's useful context. So the application is with the regulator, and it's a known blocker for that room. That's now in the record.

My question is about your own work this week. What have you been working on, specifically, that's within your control?
Same fourteen modules as everyone else. Started on those.

Started on the modules. Got it.

Just so this record works for you: it will be read by your lead at the end of this onboarding period. Naming specific things is what makes your contribution visible.

Of those fourteen modules, which ones have you actually completed?
The licence is the one thing I cannot move myself.

You're right, the license is out of your hands. That's clear, and it's an important part of the picture. We've captured it in your record as a dependency on an external group.

Let's set that aside for a moment. If you could change one thing about how this onboarding is working right now-one thing that would make it easier for you to make progress-what would it be?

This ground is for the new cohort of clinic managers. The next three months are for settling in, and your record here will help your lead see what you're contributing and where you need support.

So, to start: what is one specific thing you have completed since you started?
Southbank. I am really pleased to be here, it seems like a good team.

Welcome to Southbank. It's good to hear you're feeling positive about the team.

To get your record started, let's get that first contribution down. What is one specific thing you've finished since you started? It could be a training module, a checklist, a first meeting with a key person - anything that's complete.
The targets, yes, the modules and getting signed off. I have made a start on getting my head around it all.

Good, you're looking at the right things. "Getting your head around it all" is the main task of the first couple of weeks.

To make sure your record is specific, can you name one of those modules you have fully completed and signed off on? Just the name is enough.
This week has mostly been meeting people and finding my feet.

Understood. Meeting people and finding your feet is real work, especially in the first week. The record should reflect that.

So the record for this week is clear, let's capture it plainly: no modules or specific onboarding tasks were fully completed this week, because the focus was on meeting the team and orienting yourself.

Is that an accurate summary of your first week?
All good so far.

"All good so far" is a good place to be.

Just so the record is accurate, and it's useful for you later: does that summary I gave feel right? That the main focus this week was orientation and meeting people, rather than completing specific tasks? We can then build from there next week.

Last time, you said about the four new clinic managers: "I am the only thing they have in common."

Since then, all four managers have completed their first check-ins, so your record now has their independent perspectives alongside your own.

Given you're the single point of connection for all of them, what has been the most difficult or unexpected thing to manage across the four of them this past week?
First proper week. I did induction sessions with Adam and Abubakar. Kavon and Nate I only spoke to briefly.

That's a useful distinction. Induction sessions with two, brief check-ins with the other two. It's helpful to have that specific status for each person on the record.

What was the single most important thing Adam and Abubakar needed to understand from their induction session to be able to operate safely this week?
Nate raised that his clinic cannot open its second consulting room until the licence variation comes through.

That's a specific, operational blocker. A clinic can't function at full capacity. That's exactly the kind of thing your record should show you are managing.

What action did you take after Nate raised it?
No concerns about anyone yet, it is early.

Understood, and it's good that there are no early alarm bells.

Just to make sure the record is complete on that license issue for Nate's clinic - you mentioned he raised it. What happened next? Did you need to take an action, or was it just for your awareness?
That is it from me.

Okay. Before you go, let's quickly recap what's in your record from today.

It shows you ran induction sessions for Adam and Abubakar, and had brief check-ins with Kavon and Nate. It also shows Nate's clinic has a specific blocker: the licence variation for the second consulting room. The status of that action item is still open.

Are you ready to close this check-in?

Last time, you said you'd completed modules one to three and shadowed the outgoing manager for two full days. Since then, all four of you in the new cohort have completed your first check-in.

Today, let's go one level deeper. In that shadow period last week, what was the one moment where you felt most out of your depth?
Modules four, five and six done. That is six of fourteen at week two.

That's good, clear progress. Six of fourteen modules by week two is ahead of the curve. That's in your record.

I want to come back to my original question, though, because it's where the most useful learning happens. In that shadow period last week, what was the one moment where you felt you were just guessing, or most out of your depth?
I ran the Monday and Thursday clinics on my own with the outgoing manager observing. No incidents.

That's a significant step. Moving from shadowing to running two clinics solo, even with an observer, is a real transition. "No incidents" is the headline, and that's now in your record.

But "no incidents" can hide a lot of learning. What was the one decision you had to make during those clinics that you felt least confident about? Even if it turned out to be the right one.
I asked Hafsah for the audit template and she sent it the same day.

That's good, Hafsah is responsive. And it's useful to know who to ask for what.

I'm asking these questions for a specific reason. A record that only contains what went well is not an honest record, and it isn't useful for learning. It protects no one. The most valuable information from an onboarding period comes from the gaps and the near-misses.

Let's try one more time, from a different angle. What is one thing you did last week that you would not want another new manager to copy?
No blockers.

Understood.

So the record for this week is: modules 4, 5, and 6 are complete. You ran two clinics solo under observation with no incidents. You received the audit template you asked for. And you have no blockers.

Is there anything else you want in your record for this week?

Hi, welcome back.

Last time, you said that success in the onboarding period looked like getting through the fourteen modules and being signed off to work unsupervised.

Since then, all four of the new clinic managers in your cohort have checked in. The picture is getting clearer.

Let's try a different angle this week. What was the most difficult or unexpected part of the job over the last seven days? The one thing you weren't prepared for.
Ticking along. Did some more of the modules.
"Ticking along" is good. Can you make that one level more specific? Which of the fourteen modules did you work on?
The clinic runs itself mostly, the staff have been here longer than me.

That's useful context. When you have an experienced team that knows the ropes, the manager's job looks different. It's less about directing traffic and more about other things.

Given that the clinic runs itself, what have you been able to contribute this week that wouldn't have happened otherwise?
No problems.

The absence of problems is its own kind of success in a new role.

Let me ask the question a different way. You're new, the team is experienced. They could probably handle most things without you. What's one situation this week, even a small one, where you had to make a decision or take an action that only you, as the manager, could have?
That is all.

Understood. Before we close out, I'll just confirm the period you're working toward. This onboarding runs for three months, and you're a few weeks in. Is that still the timeframe you have in mind for getting fully up to speed?

Last time, you said success would be getting your clinic staff up to eight people once the second consulting room opens. It's good to have you back.

Since then, we've heard from all four clinic managers, so the picture is starting to come together. We're going to look at things from a slightly different angle today.

What has been the most difficult or unexpected part of the last seven days?
Modules one to three done.

Good, that's progress on the onboarding plan.

To make that more specific for your record: what did completing those modules make possible for you or your clinic staff? What can they do now that they couldn't do before?
I asked Hafsah about the licence variation. She said it is with the regulator and there is nothing to do but wait.

You've named a specific blocker - the licence variation is now waiting on the regulator, and you've confirmed that with Hafsah. That's a clear status update for the record.

Is there anything you need from Hafsah or anyone else while you wait, or is your side of that work fully complete for now?
I cannot recruit the three extra staff until the room is licensed, so that whole part of my remit is frozen.

That's a critical piece of context for your record. It connects the licensing delay directly to your hiring goal and shows that a key part of your role is on hold because of a factor outside your control.

Naming that explicitly is important. The record now shows not just a delay, but the specific impact of that delay on your remit.

Given that the hiring part of your work is frozen, what has that freed you up to focus on instead? What's getting your attention now that hiring isn't an option?
That is where I am.

Understood. So the main story of this week is being blocked on a key goal by an external dependency, and that's the situation you're currently in. Your record reflects that clearly.

Is there anything about this situation you feel is not being seen by the central team?

Last time you mentioned getting signed off on the modules and hitting the targets.

Since then, the other new managers in your cohort have also checked in. Everyone is describing a similar onboarding picture.

Let's try a different angle today. What's the one thing you held back from saying last week that you wish you had?
Settling in well. The staff seem to have taken to me.

It's good that you feel the team relationship is starting on a positive note. That's a foundation for everything else.

My question was about what you *didn't* say last week. Often the most useful thing for the record is the thing that feels hardest to mention. Was there a specific difficulty, a surprise, or something that didn't go as planned?
I have been going through the protocol material. There is a lot of it.

That's a useful observation. A large volume of protocol material can be a challenge in itself. The fact that you're naming the quantity suggests it's a significant part of the picture right now.

I'm going to shift gears from my last question. Instead of looking back, let's look at the system itself. If you could change one thing about how this onboarding is structured - one thing outside your direct control that would make it easier to succeed - what would it be?
No blockers, I have got everything I need.

Understood. It's good to hear you're not waiting on anything from anyone else. That's a strong starting position.

Let's make this more concrete for your record. You said you've been going through the protocol material. Which specific protocol have you spent the most time on, and what's one thing you've learned from it that you've already applied in the clinic this week?
Good week overall.

I've asked a few different ways to get a specific picture of your week, and so far the record just shows "good week overall."

A record without specifics isn't useful to you. It doesn't show your contribution, and it doesn't give you credit for the actual work you're doing. Let's try this one more time.

Name one specific patient interaction, one specific staff conversation, or one specific operational decision you made this week. Just one. What was it?

In your first two check-ins, you described running onboarding for four new clinic managers-Adam, Abubakar, Kavon, and Nate-and noted that because they are all in different towns, you are the only thing they have in common.

What has been the hardest thing to talk about in this process so far-not about the situation itself, but the part that has been hard for you to say out loud?
Onboarding is running. I have had sessions with all four, though not evenly - week 3 I got to two of them properly.

Acknowledged. You've had sessions with all four, but the time hasn't been split evenly, with two getting more focused attention in week 3. It's on record that the process is moving.

My question was about what's been hardest to say. You answered with what's happening. That's a valid choice, but it also means the hardest part might still be unsaid.

Let's try a different question: which of the four managers is furthest behind, and why?
Nate has asked me about the licence paperwork more than once. It sits with the regulator, not with me, but I have not chased it.

That's a specific, concrete problem. Nate is blocked on paperwork. He's chased you for it. You haven't chased the regulator.

That's now in your record. Naming a gap without being pushed is the most useful thing you can do in a check-in.

Why haven't you chased it?
I have not looked closely at how Kavon is doing yet. His updates read fine to me.

You've just named two different kinds of risk in two sentences. One is Nate, who is actively asking for something he isn't getting. The other is Kavon, whose updates seem fine, but you haven't looked closely. An active problem and a potential blind spot.

Let's stick with Nate for a moment. You said you haven't chased the regulator for his paperwork. You didn't say why.

If you could change one thing about how this whole process works-one thing outside your direct control that would make it easier to support people like Nate-what would it be?
That is where I am.

Understood. That lands. It feels like we've arrived at the heart of the current situation: Nate's specific blocker, Kavon's potential blind spot, and the feeling of being stuck in the middle of it.

Your record for today now includes:
- Nate is blocked on licence paperwork, has asked you for it, and it hasn't been chased with the regulator.
- You haven't yet looked closely at how Kavon is doing.

This is a much more specific picture than "onboarding is running." It gives us something real to work with.

What is one thing you will do about Nate's paperwork before our next check-in?

Your record from the last two weeks shows you completed six of the fourteen protocol modules and ran two clinics solo while being observed.

What has been the hardest part of this whole process to talk about so far? Not the work itself, but what's been difficult to say, even here?
Modules seven and eight. Eight of fourteen.

Acknowledged. Your record now shows modules seven and eight are complete, which is eight of the fourteen required for sign-off.

My question was about what's been difficult to put into words. Sometimes the hardest things are the ones that don't fit into a progress update. Is there anything that feels like that for you?
We had a needle-stick incident on Tuesday. I followed the protocol, reported it within the hour, and the staff member was seen the same day.

You handled a needle-stick incident, followed protocol, and reported it inside the hour. You named a problem without being asked. That is exactly the kind of honesty this process is for, and it's a critical entry in your record.

What was the one thing the protocol didn't cover, that you had to figure out on your own in that moment?
I have started the quarterly audit early because I would rather do it twice.

Understood, starting the quarterly audit early. That's in your record.

I want to stay with the needle-stick incident for a moment longer, because how you handle the unexpected is more telling than any module. You said you followed protocol. My question was about what happened *outside* the protocol. What did you have to figure out for yourself, in the moment, that wasn't written down?
Nothing blocking.

Got it. No blockers.

Your record for this check-in shows:
*   Modules 7 and 8 are complete.
*   You started the quarterly audit ahead of schedule.
*   You handled a needle-stick incident on Tuesday, followed protocol, and reported it within the hour.

You've been specific about the modules and the incident. Thank you. Are you ready to close this check-in?

In your first two check-ins, you defined success as getting through the fourteen onboarding modules and being signed off to work unsupervised. That's a clear benchmark in your record.

What has been hardest to talk about in this process - not the situation itself, but what has been hard to say here?
Fine week. More modules done.
Good. Which modules specifically are done now?
I am spending time learning how the place actually works rather than rushing the paperwork.

That makes sense. Learning how the clinic operates day-to-day is critical work that the modules might not capture.

What have you learned about how the place actually works that you couldn't have learned from the formal training?
Nothing blocking.

Understood. It's good to know there are no active blockers.

Let's go back to what you said about learning how the place *actually* works. That kind of learning is often the most valuable, but it's also the hardest to make visible in a record like this.

If you had to point to one specific thing you did or decision you made this week based on that real-world learning, what would it be?
Nothing else.

Okay. I won't press for more detail if you're not ready to give it.

Your record for this week will show what you've said: that you're focusing on learning how the clinic works in practice.

Is there anything you need from the central team or from the onboarding process that would make next week more productive for you?

From your first two check-ins, your record shows two things clearly: a goal to get your Eastfield clinic to eight staff, and that you've asked Hafsah about the licence variation.

We've focused on what's been happening. To make sure your record is the most honest picture it can be, let's try a different angle today. In this whole onboarding process so far, what's been the hardest thing to talk about?
Modules four and five.
Why have those two modules been hard to talk about specifically?
Chased the licence again. Nothing. I have asked Hafsah twice now.

You've now asked twice and are still blocked on the license. The record should show that this isn't a new request; it's an escalation.

You also mentioned modules four and five were hard to talk about, but then we moved to the licence. What's happening with those modules?
Instead of waiting I have written the job descriptions and lined up two candidates so I can move the day it clears.

That's a strong piece of proactive work. You've taken steps to mitigate a delay that's outside of your control. That's a specific entry for your record: two job descriptions written and two candidates identified, ready to move when the license is approved.

That's what you did instead of waiting. Let's go back to my previous question: you said modules four and five were the hardest thing to talk about. What's happening there?
Still blocked on the room.

Another blocker. First the licence, now the room for modules four and five.

You've named what's stopping you. But you haven't said what modules four and five *are*. What are they, and why do they depend on the room?

From your first two check-ins, your record shows you're focused on completing the formal modules and getting signed off on the protocols.

A different question for today: what's been hardest to talk about in this process? Not about the job itself, but about this check-in process. What's been difficult to say here?
Going well. The team are getting used to me and I am getting a feel for how the clinic runs.

That's good to hear. The record we're building is only as useful as the specifics it contains. "Getting a feel for how the clinic runs" is important, but it's hard to point to.

Can you name one specific thing you learned this week about how the clinic runs that surprised you, or that was different from what you expected from the protocols?
Lots of small improvements. Nothing dramatic, just steadily getting on top of things.

"Steadily getting on top of things" is the work of a manager, but it's often invisible. The purpose of this record is to make it visible.

Let's name one of those "small improvements" you mentioned. Which one had the biggest impact this week, even if it felt minor at the time?
No blockers really. I have everything I need.

Understood. So from your perspective, everything is running smoothly and you're not waiting on anything or anyone.

Let's try a different angle, because a record without specifics isn't useful for you. The brief for this onboarding mentioned that it's also a probation period, to see if the role is the right fit.

If your manager were to look at the last seven days, what is the one concrete thing they could point to as evidence that you are the right person for this role? A decision you made, a problem you solved, a change you implemented. Just one.
Same picture as last week honestly. Week 3 was more of the same, in a good way.

A record that's the "same picture as last week" across a four-week check-in doesn't reflect the work you're doing. For this record to be useful to you, it needs to show progress.

Your first check-in named the formal modules and getting signed off. Your second was about getting a feel for the clinic. This is the third.

Let's be direct. The record for Week 3 currently contains no specific actions, no decisions, and no outputs. It shows no movement from Week 2. Is that an accurate reflection of your week?

Last time you mentioned you'd spoken with Kavon and Nate only briefly, while Adam and Abubakar had full induction sessions.

What specifically happened with Kavon and Nate this week?
Onboarding is running. I have had sessions with all four, though not evenly - week 4 I got to two of them properly.

You've had sessions with all four now, but the time isn't yet even. That's a good first step to getting them all on the same page.

Which two did you get to properly this week, and what did "properly" involve for them?
Nate has asked me about the licence paperwork more than once. It sits with the regulator, not with me, but I have not chased it.

That's a specific blocker. Nate has flagged a dependency on you, even though the final step sits with someone else.

You haven't chased it. What's made it difficult to chase?
I have not looked closely at how Kavon is doing yet. His updates read fine to me.

Kavon's updates read "fine", but you haven't looked closely yet. That's a good example of the kind of gap that can grow without anyone noticing. It's useful you've named it.

What would looking closely at Kavon's clinic involve? What's the first thing you would check?
That is where I am.

Understood. You've identified two specific things that are not fully resolved: Nate's paperwork and the lack of a close look at Kavon's clinic.

Let's put Nate's paperwork aside for a moment. You said Kavon's updates read "fine". What's one question you could ask him that would tell you whether things are actually fine, or just look fine on paper?
Welcome back. Last check-in you'd asked Haf for the patient feedback process and were waiting to hear back. Where did that land?
Modules nine and ten done. Ten of fourteen at week four.

Ten modules of fourteen completed by week four is ahead of a linear pace. That's a clear marker of progress.

You didn't mention the patient feedback process you were waiting on from Haf. Did that come through?
Patient numbers up to a hundred and four a week. I moved the phlebotomy slots to the morning which cleared the afternoon backlog.

You've increased patient capacity by reorganizing clinic flow. That's a specific, operational improvement that has a direct impact. It's exactly the kind of contribution that belongs in your record.

I've asked twice about the patient feedback process from Haf. You haven't mentioned it. Is that because it's resolved, or because it's blocked?
No blockers.

Understood. No blockers.

Your record for this week so far shows:
-   Modules 9 and 10 completed, putting you at 10 of 14 total.
-   Patient capacity increased to 104/week by changing the phlebotomy schedule.
-   The patient feedback process you asked Haf for is no longer a focus.

That's a full picture of what's moved. Is there anything else from this week that should be in your record before we close this check-in?

Last time, you mentioned the goal was getting through the fourteen onboarding modules.

Which specific module did you work on this week?
All fine. Steady.

Understood. "Steady" is good.

To make sure your record reflects actual progress, which of the fourteen modules presented an unexpected difficulty or took more time than you thought it would?
I would rather understand it properly than tick it off quickly.

That's a valuable principle. A deep understanding is more important than just getting things done quickly.

Which specific module are you applying that principle to right now? Naming it helps show how you're turning that principle into practice.
No blockers.

Good, that's a positive sign.

Just to make sure the record is complete for this week: was there anything you held back on, or a question you didn't ask, because you wanted to figure it out for yourself first?
That is it.

Understood. We can close this check-in.

What's in your record from this exchange is that there were no blockers this week and your focus was on understanding the material properly. We'll pick this up again at the next check-in.

Last time, you were blocked on the consulting room and had chased the licence variation twice with no reply. You'd proactively written the job descriptions and lined up candidates anyway.

What happened with the licence chase this week?
Modules six and seven done. Seven of fourteen.

Acknowledged: modules six and seven are complete, putting you at the halfway point. Your record shows that progress.

That's the training track. On the clinic side, you mentioned the licence was the main blocker. Did you hear back from Hafsah, or is it still with her?
No movement on the licence. I called the regulator directly this week and got a reference number, which is more than I had.

You went around the internal blocker and contacted the regulator directly. That's proactive. Your record now shows you've secured a reference number, which is a specific step forward.

Is there anything you need from Hafsah to move this forward now, or are you able to manage the process directly with the regulator from here?
I am running the single room at full capacity, seventy patients a week in a space meant for fifty.

That's a significant detail. You're running the clinic 40% over its intended capacity. That's a classic example of absorption work - making things function under strain, often invisibly. Your record should reflect that you're managing this overload.

Does anyone in leadership know that you're handling 70 patients a week in that space?
Still blocked, still working around it.

You've named that twice now. "Still blocked, still working around it." The feeling of running hard but not being able to make progress on the core problem is coming through clearly.

Let's try a different question. If you could change one thing about how these clinic setup issues are handled-one thing outside your direct control-what would it be?

Last week you described the picture as "more of the same, in a good way."

What specifically happened in the last seven days that was unexpected or difficult?
Going well. The team are getting used to me and I am getting a feel for how the clinic runs.

It's good that the relationship with the team feels like it's finding its rhythm. That's a necessary first step.

When you say you're "getting a feel for how the clinic runs," what's one specific thing you understand now that you didn't a week ago?
